stories.title: LOFAR delivers an ultra-deep sub-arcsecond image of the ELAIS-N1 radio sky
paragraphs: In an arXiv preprint accepted for Astronomy & Astrophysics, J.M.G.H.J. de Jong (Leiden Observatory/ASTRON) and collaborators present ultra-deep sub-arcsecond radio images of the ELAIS-N1 field from 200 hours of LOFAR High-Band Antenna observations at 115–168 MHz over a 2.5×2.5 square-degree area.

According to the paper, the highest-resolution mosaic reaches a central point-source sensitivity of 5.3 μJy beam−1 at 0.33″×0.39″ (area-weighted 7.4 μJy beam−1 at 0.36″×0.45″). Combining the new data with prior deep 6″ LOFAR images yields a catalogue of 62,916 unique radio sources. The authors call these among the deepest radio images below 1.28 GHz and among the deepest at any radio frequency.

The preprint says recent long-baseline calibration and imaging advances made processing this volume feasible, with astrometric alignment to Gaia quasars giving milliarcsecond-level offsets. The team frames the release as a benchmark for wider LOFAR2.0 and Square Kilometre Array–era deep surveys. An ADASS 2026 talk abstract by the same effort notes the 200-hour set corresponds to about 400 TB of visibility data.

stories.title: Blind listeners and musicians show less internal noise in pitch hearing
paragraphs: In The Conversation, Georgia Tech psychologist Woon Ju Park summarizes a Journal of Neuroscience study comparing nine people blind before age 2 with 18 sighted participants who had varied musical training on tone-in-noise detection and pitch discrimination tasks.

Park writes that early-blind participants outperformed sighted peers only on pitch discrimination, pointing to brain-level processing rather than cochlear frequency selectivity. A mathematical model attributed the advantage to lower internal noise—more consistent responses to the same sound over time.

The same analysis found that musical training similarly reduced internal noise in sighted musicians compared with people who were neither early-blind nor extensively trained. Park says how much training is needed, and whether gains extend to everyday complex listening, remains open.

stories.title: SLAC-led team confirms altermagnetism, a third class of magnetism, in manganese telluride
paragraphs: ScienceDaily and SLAC report that a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory published experimental evidence in Science for altermagnetism, a magnetic phase distinct from ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Lead author Daniel Jost said the results provide "robust experimental confirmation that this third phase—altermagnetism—is real." The paper, "Chiral altermagnon in MnTe," is dated Oct. 29, 2026.

According to SLAC and Phys.org, the researchers studied manganese telluride (MnTe), long classified as an antiferromagnet. Altermagnets are described as having alternating electron spins like antiferromagnets, but with crystal structures around opposite spins rotated relative to each other—a symmetry break proposed when the term was introduced in 2022.

The team used circularly polarized X-rays at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility's ID32 beamline. SLAC says chiral materials scatter left- and right-handed polarized beams differently; MnTe showed that chiral signature, which conventional antiferromagnets should not. The measurements were first made in 2024 and repeated in early 2025.

Jost told SLAC that ferromagnets are easily disturbed by stray magnetic fields, while antiferromagnets are hard to read or drive with spin currents. "Altermagnets combine the best of both," he said: zero net magnetization with the ability to generate spin-polarized currents. The work received partial DOE Office of Science support.

image.credit: Greg Stewart/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, via ScienceDaily

stories.title: Voyager 1 resumes contact after a 48-hour communications pause
paragraphs: JPL said NASA's Deep Space Network lost Voyager 1's signal on Oct. 18–19, 2026, then regained it on Oct. 20 after about 48 hours, before troubleshooting commands could arrive. Space.com notes the probe is nearly one light-day from Earth and will hit that distance on Nov. 18.

Engineers found one thruster group went offline and backups engaged automatically under fault protection. Mission manager Kareem Badaruddin called it the first time the spacecraft has behaved this way. The root cause remains under investigation.

In early September, JPL finished Voyager 1's "Big Bang" power swap—replacing three devices with lower-power alternatives—after a similar change on Voyager 2 about six weeks earlier, aiming to keep remaining science instruments running longer as each craft loses about 4 watts of power per year.
